analysis.file_name: Morgan Stanley - Living on the Edge, The Rise of Distributed Power - Oct 6 2026.pdf
analysis.title: Living on the Edge: The Rise of Distributed Power
key_insights: Morgan Stanley argues the AI buildout is colliding with a grid that cannot deliver power fast enough. A growing power shortfall, political pushback on data centers and the shift from training to inference push power and compute toward the edge. It calls behind-the-meter (BTM) power a structural architectural shift, not a bridge solution.

MS forecasts a ~120 GW, or $240bn, power equipment total addressable market (TAM) for BTM solutions through 2029, made up of 77 GW for data centers and 40 GW for commercial and industrial (C&I) customers.

US data center power shortfall: MS Thematics forecasts 160 GW of incremental data center power demand in 2026-2029. 22 GW is already under construction with a grid connection, and MS estimates 36 GW of available US grid capacity. 23 GW of BTM equipment has been procured by developers (SEI, PUMP, WMB, LBRT, HAL/VoltaGrid). That leaves a 77 GW shortfall to be filled by BTM solutions.

MS introduces the Stranded Compute Adjusted Cost of Power (SCACP). It adds a stranded compute premium (the cost of GPUs, capital and contracted revenue sitting idle until energized) to the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). The premium assumes $4,500/kW of economic benefit per year of accelerated grid connection, about $42/MWh per year of expedited access over a 15-year project life.
Grid power has the lowest LCOE but the highest SCACP because interconnection takes 5-7 years. Fast-to-deploy technologies can justify higher headline power costs.

BTM composite ranking today: Bloom Energy's solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) ranks #1 (4.5/5, SCACP $131/MWh), micro turbine generator (BorgWarner) #2 (3.7, $135), retrofitted CFM56 aeroderivative (FTAI) #3 (3.4, $132), fast-start reciprocating gas engine #4 (3.3, $189) and industrial gas turbine #5 (1.8, $258). Weights are 50% SCACP, 15% noise/NIMBY, 15% technology maturity, and 10% each for load following and emissions.

With no time-to-power premium (2030 view), the ranking changes and the range narrows. Reciprocating gas engines rank #1 (3.8, LCOE $110/MWh), SOFC #2 (3.8, $116), aeroderivative #3 (3.7, $104), micro turbine #4 (3.5, $111) and industrial gas turbine #5 (1.6, $144). MS ties this to the market debate over how long the acute time-to-power problem lasts.

MS expects hybrid configurations, a fast thermal source paired with storage for transient response and load following, to become the default onsite architecture. US energy storage system (ESS) annual deployments are forecast at 279 GWh by 2030, a 38% CAGR from 2025, including 169 GWh of annual data center demand. Cumulative US installed ESS is projected near 1,000 GWh by 2030, against ~90 GWh in 2024.

Virtual power plants (VPPs) are scaling. On September 9, 2026, Sunrun and Tesla coordinated more than 140,000 residential batteries to deliver over 580 MW to the California grid for a three-hour evening dispatch. 517 MW came from about 110,000 Tesla Powerwalls and 63 MW from other makers. A day later they supplied another 140+ MW at Southern California Edison's request.

In June 2026 Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home signed a non-binding framework to aggregate more than 16 GW of flexible capacity for utilities and hyperscalers. They cite 300+ MW of potentially flexible resources in Virginia, possibly 500 MW by 2030.

Supply vs demand: MS estimates 149 GW of primary-power gas equipment supply by 2030, which supports 120 GW of data center power with 20% overbuild. MS's data center model has ~150 GW of incremental demand by 2030. The model shows a supply surplus of 19.9 GW in 2027 and 4.8 GW in 2028, then a shortage of 15.1 GW in 2029 and 29.2 GW in 2030.

Evidence supply stays tight: prices are rising for large-frame and industrial gas turbines, slot-reservation down payments are up to 25% for 2030 large-frame delivery, and project sizes are growing with multiple >2 GW projects announced. INIO and CAT are fully booked through 2028, with 2030 the pivot point.

MS thinks supply may be overstated and demand understated in 2030. Some equipment is destined for non-data-center markets, new-entrant capacity is speculative, and onsite power needs 10-35% overbuild. Some new-entrant technology may be used as temporary bridge power rather than prime power.

MS forecasts ~10 GW of incremental US C&I demand annually through 2030, additive to the BTM TAM (9.8 GW in 2027E rising to 13.3 GW in 2035E). Reshoring is a driver: if the US share of global manufacturing returns to 20% by 2050 from 16% in 2025, up to 113 GW of incremental electricity capacity is needed through 2035.

Political pushback supports BTM. Third parties estimate ~$156bn of data center projects were cancelled or delayed in 2025 and $130bn in 1Q26. Moratorium proposals are spreading across Democratic, Republican and divided states. Texas is auditing 474 GW of pending ERCOT requests (~90% data center), Virginia's July 31 Rider T1 order moves Dominion toward 'cost causer pays', and Pennsylvania's governor ended fast-track permitting and required local approval.

MS says the grid still matters. Combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs) or the grid are best suited to mega-campuses of 1 GW+ used for training. Modular solutions (fuel cells, small turbines) gain ground as inference moves to smaller edge nodes.

Physical AI is a longer-term distributed layer. Vehicles, robots and drones with onboard compute could form a Distributed Inference Cloud, with robot/EV compute capacity estimated at ~1.0 TW by 2040. Battery-equipped assets can also act as distributed power.

MS top ideas, onsite power equipment: Bloom Energy (BE), Baker Hughes (BKR), BorgWarner (BWA, with a corresponding upgrade), Cummins (CMI), ERock (EROC), FTAI Aviation (FTAI), INNIO (INIO) and Rolls Royce (RR). Onsite power developers: Solaris (SEI), Liberty (LBRT), Halliburton (HAL), Williams (WMB). Key ESS/VPP providers: Tesla (TSLA), Ford (F), Fluence (FLNC), BorgWarner (BWA), Sunrun (RUN).

market_movers.rationale: Bloom's SOFC ranks #1 on MS's BTM composite (4.5/5) on fastest time to power (<6 months), 800V DC output, load following and low noise and emissions. Its LCOE is at the high end of the cost curve.
BorgWarner's TurboCell micro turbine generator ranks #2 (3.7/5) on the BTM scorecard, and the report points to a corresponding BWA upgrade. BWA is also listed as a key ESS/VPP provider.
FTAI's retrofitted CFM56 aeroderivative genset ranks #3 (3.4/5) with SCACP of $132/MWh and the lowest 2030 no-premium LCOE of the group ($104/MWh).
Fast-start reciprocating gas engines rank #4 today but #1 on the 2030 no-time-premium view. INIO is fully booked through 2028 with pricing and shipments locked in.
ERock is a named top idea among reciprocating gas engine suppliers, a segment that screens best on cost once time-to-power normalizes.
Cummins is a named top idea in reciprocating gas engines, tied to the 77 GW BTM shortfall.

Baker Hughes is the top idea for industrial gas turbines (NovaLT), which rank last on the composite (1.8/5) and have the highest SCACP ($258/MWh). MS still lists it as a top idea for onsite power equipment.
Rolls Royce (mtu gas gensets) is listed among MS's top ideas for onsite power equipment suppliers.
Solaris is a top idea among onsite power developers, and its procured BTM equipment is part of the 23 GW expected at data center sites.
Liberty is a top idea among onsite power developers, with procured BTM equipment counted in the 23 GW.
Halliburton (with VoltaGrid) is a top idea among onsite power developers, with procured BTM equipment counted in the 23 GW.
Williams is a top idea among onsite power developers, with procured BTM equipment counted in the 23 GW.
Tesla is a key ESS/VPP provider. About 110,000 Powerwalls supplied 517 MW of the 580 MW California dispatch on September 9.
Sunrun owned and operated 55% of the participating Powerwalls and dispatched more than 30,000 additional customer batteries in the September 9 California VPP event.
Fluence is listed as a key ESS/VPP provider, with US ESS deployments forecast at 279 GWh by 2030.
Ford is listed as a key ESS/VPP provider through vehicle-to-grid and storage exposure.

sector_views.rationale: The coverage banner shows an Industry View of In-Line. The report treats vehicles as potential distributed inference and power nodes over the long run.
The report is bullish on behind-the-meter power, storage and VPPs. It also says the grid keeps a major role, especially for 1 GW+ training campuses.
Onsite power developers (SEI, LBRT, HAL, WMB) and gas equipment suppliers are named top ideas, supported by tight turbine and engine supply and rising prices.
The report flags rising demand for onsite power equipment (BKR, CMI, EROC, INIO, FTAI, BWA). It also links onshoring to additional C&I power demand.

risk_factors: The time-to-power premium may shrink if equipment supply becomes abundant. In the 2030 no-time-premium view the ranking shifts toward reciprocating engines and the SOFC advantage narrows.
Onsite power supply and demand are not well understood. New-entrant capacity could add supply, and some new-entrant technology may serve temporary bridge power, which affects pricing.
Bloom's SOFC sits at the high end of the cost curve ($3,500/kW capex, $225/kW-yr fixed O&M), so its ranking depends on the time-to-power advantage.
Political pushback and moratoriums could slow data center build-outs, although MS notes most efforts aim to slow rather than reverse them.
SMRs have no commercially available units today and face 5-10 year timelines.
Solar plus storage is less common in BTM today because of land needs and intermittency.
The composite ranking depends on MS's weightings (50% SCACP), and developers with different priorities could rank technologies differently.
Large-scale mega-campuses of 1 GW+ may still rely on CCGTs or the grid, which limits the BTM opportunity there.
charts_described: Exhibit 2/10: US data center power shortfall through 2029 (midpoint) steps from 160.0 GW total demand, less 21.8 GW under construction, 36.2 GW utility grid access, 22.8 GW BTM turbines/engines in backlog and 2.8 GW nuclear plant siting (probability-weighted), to a 76.5 GW net shortfall.

Exhibit 3/12: Stranded compute adjusted cost of power by technology. BTM LCOE: SOFC $131, aeroderivative $111, micro turbine $114, gas reciprocating $104, industrial gas turbine $131, grid $89/MWh. Stranded premiums are $21, $21, $85, $127 and $233/MWh for the BTM technologies, giving totals of $131-$258 for those and $323 for grid.
Exhibit 7/20: US energy storage demand. Non-data-center demand runs from 57 GWh (2025) to 110 GWh (2030E). Data center ESS demand reaches 169 GWh by 2030E.
Exhibit 9/25: Potential US incremental C&I demand rises from 9.8 GW (2027E) to 13.3 GW (2035E).
geopolitical: US political pushback on data centers is rising ahead of the midterm elections, centered on power bills, water and air pollution, and noise.
State and local data center moratorium proposals are appearing roughly evenly in Democratic trifectas, Republican trifectas and divided governments.
Pennsylvania issued an executive order ending fast-track permitting for data centers, requiring local approval and requiring projects to bring their own capacity.
Texas is auditing data centers in ERCOT's interconnection queue, which has more than 474 GW of pending requests.
Virginia's July 31 Rider T1 order moves Dominion toward 'cost causer pays' for direct-connect transmission.
Ohio's Vivek Ramaswamy 'Ohioans-First' proposal is not current law and MS reads it as a sentiment indicator.

tension_points.bull_case: MS sees ~150 GW of incremental data center demand by 2030 against 149 GW of gas equipment supply, which supports 120 GW after 20% overbuild. That implies a 29.2 GW shortage in 2030. Prices are rising, down payments reach 25% for 2030 large-frame delivery, and INIO and CAT are booked through 2028.
tension_points.bear_case: Industry debate is whether onsite power ends up oversupplied. MS's own model shows a surplus of 19.9 GW in 2027 and 4.8 GW in 2028. New entrants are adding speculative capacity, and the time-to-power premium narrows if supply becomes abundant.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 2030 supply/demand balance that tips into surplus, for example new-entrant capacity that proves real and competes for prime power, would weaken the case. The report does not give a specific level.

tension_points.bull_case: Fast deployment justifies higher headline costs, so SOFC ranks #1 today despite a higher LCOE than gas engines. Grid interconnection takes 5-7 years.
tension_points.bear_case: With no time premium (2030), reciprocating gas engines and SOFC tie at 3.8/5 and engines lead on cost, so the SOFC edge narrows when supply is abundant.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Equipment becoming freely available, so the time-to-power gap closes, would remove the SOFC ranking advantage.

theme_stances.key_argument: Power scarcity, political pushback and the shift to inference make behind-the-meter power a durable architectural shift, not a bridge.
theme_stances.evidence: we do not believe behind-the-meter power is merely a bridge solution

theme_stances.key_argument: Batteries smooth sub-second GPU transients and enable peak shaving, so hybrid thermal-plus-storage setups become the default onsite architecture.
theme_stances.evidence: hybrid configurations to become the default onsite architecture

theme_stances.key_argument: Pricing is rising, down payments are growing and 2030 supply may be overstated, which keeps MS bullish on supply and demand.
theme_stances.evidence: thus keeping us bullish on supply/demand dynamics
